about: Real words, phrases and sentences from public-domain novels (Project Gutenberg) that are hard to picture without help. Used by scripts/illustrate_showcase.py to test POST /illustrate. Quotes are exact; only public-domain books, never copyrighted text (CLAUDE.md).

expectations.title: Great Expectations
expectations.author: Charles Dickens
expectations.setting_era: the Kent marshes, England, in the 1810s

examples.why_hard: Latin-looking word for the waxy oil from a sperm whale's head, once used for candles.
Ship's term: the stand that holds the compass near the wheel.
French word with an accent for a light horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood.
Rough cart that carried prisoners to the guillotine; grim, so the picture must stay calm.
Water pipe for smoking; the Caterpillar's, but readers may not know the object.
Also a Greek myth name; here a light open carriage pulled by ponies.
Misleading: it is a heavy walking stick, not a lawyer. Without context a picture is likely to get this wrong.
A two-wheeled horse-drawn cab with the driver sitting high at the back.
Possessive plus a hyphenated object few readers have seen: a shackle for a prisoner's ankle.
Moreen is an old heavy ribbed fabric; the colour and material both have to show.

examples.text: It was a fine, thick piece of wood, bulbous-headed, of the sort which is known as a “Penang lawyer.”
examples.why_hard: Same phrase as above, now with its sentence: does the context turn the lawyer into a walking stick?

examples.text: Lighting the pipe at the binnacle lamp and planting the stool on the weather side of the deck, he sat and smoked.
examples.why_hard: Two ship terms (binnacle, weather side) and a long opening clause before the action.

examples.text: The try-works are planted between the foremast and mainmast, the most roomy part of the deck.
examples.why_hard: Describes a thing almost nobody has seen: brick furnaces on deck for boiling whale blubber.

examples.text: When the calèche stopped, the driver jumped down and held out his hand to assist me to alight.
examples.why_hard: Accented foreign word plus the old-fashioned verb 'alight' (to get down).

examples.text: I mounted into the window-seat: gathering up my feet, I sat cross-legged, like a Turk; and, having drawn the red moreen curtain nearly close, I was shrined in double retirement.
examples.why_hard: 30 words, heavy punctuation, and 'shrined in double retirement' means hidden away, not a shrine.

examples.text: And on the ground beside her, when Joe picked her up, was a convict’s leg-iron which had been filed asunder.
examples.why_hard: The scene follows an attack; 'filed asunder' means cut in two. The picture must stay calm.

examples.text: Six tumbrils carry the day’s wine to La Guillotine.
examples.why_hard: A metaphor: the 'wine' is the condemned prisoners. Read literally, it means barrels of wine.

examples.text: In a moment they were all out of the chaise, rejoicing at the sight of each other.
examples.why_hard: 'Chaise' (a small closed carriage) is easy to read as 'chase' or a chair.
Repeat of the first word with a capital letter: should come back instantly from the cache.

examples.text: Besides her hoisted boats, an American whaler is outwardly distinguished by her try-works. The try-works are planted between the foremast and mainmast, the most roomy part of the deck.
examples.why_hard: Two sentences from the page at once: the app should send one at a time.
A line from the table of contents, as OCR would read it.

examples.text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
examples.why_hard: The famous opening: more than one sentence and over 200 characters.
